messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.02 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.15 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.01 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Interface circuit for a piezoelectric energy harvester.
    *   Output target: $1.8\text{ V} \le V_{\text{out}} \le 3.6\text{ V}$, ripple $\le 20\text{ mV}$, startup $t_{\text{up}} \le 0.15\text{ s}$, settled $\Delta V \le 0.01\text{ V}$.
    *   Operating Conditions: S1 (nom), S2 (heavy load), S3 (strong exc/light load), S4 (weak exc), S5 (low freq), S6 (hot/Cp+20%).
    *   Piezo Model: Current source $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$ in parallel with $C_p$ and $20\text{ M}\Omega$.
    *   Key constraints:
        *   $V_{\text{oc\_amp}} \approx 3.2\text{ V}$ at S1.
        *   Cold start from $0\text{ V}$.
        *   $V_{\text{out\_min}} = 1.8\text{ V}$, $V_{\text{out\_max}} = 3.6\text{ V}$.
        *   Load $R_L$ varies from $150\text{ k}\Omega$ to $2200\text{ k}\Omega$.
        *   $C_p = 25\text{--}30\text{ nF}$.
    *   Reference design (FBR) failed on ripple, startup, and stability (settled). S3 overshot $V_{\text{out\_max}}$. S2 and S4 didn't reach $V_{\text{out\_min}}$.

    *   $V_{\text{oc}}$ is low ($\approx 3.2\text{ V}$ peak). A full-bridge rectifier (FBR) has two diode drops (~$0.5\text{ V}$ total for DSCH).
    *   $V_{\text{out}}$ is clamped by the piezo voltage.
    *   The ripple is too high with just a capacitor.
    *   S3 (strong excitation) leads to overvoltage ($V_{\text{out}} > 3.6\text{ V}$). This suggests a need for a zener clamp or a regulator.
    *   S4 (weak excitation) fails to reach $1.8\text{ V}$ with FBR. This suggests the need for a boost-like mechanism or better efficiency (SSHI).

    *   **Topology 1: SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor).**
        *   Standard SSHI uses a switch and an inductor to invert the voltage across $C_p$ at the peaks. This significantly increases the harvested energy by reducing the effect of $C_p$.
        *   Configuration: Parallel SSHI or Series SSHI.
        *   Parallel SSHI: Piezo $\to$ Rectifier $\to$ Capacitor. The switch/inductor loop is across the piezo.
        *   Wait, the components allowed are `S`, `SYNC`, `L`, `D`, `C`, `R`.
        *   A simple Parallel SSHI:
            *   Rectifier (half-bridge or full-bridge).
            *   A switch $S_1$ and inductor $L_1$ to invert $V_{pzp}$ and $V_{pzn}$.
            *   Or a simpler version: $L$ in series with $S$ and the piezo.
        *   Actually, for Parallel SSHI: The switch and inductor are placed in parallel with the piezo to flip the voltage $V_{Cp}$ at the peaks.
        *   But the provided components allow a more integrated approach. Let's try a "Half-bridge SSHI" or "Synchronous Rectifier".
        *   Wait, the most robust way to handle the $V_{\text{out}}$ constraints is a combination of SSHI (for energy) and a Zener clamp (to prevent overvoltage).

    *   **Topology 2: Boost Converter / Charge Pump.**
        *   Too complex for the limited components and the specific `SYNC` controller. `SYNC` is designed for peak-flipping (L-Cp inversion).

    *   **Topology 3: SECE (Synchronized Electric Charge Extraction).**
        *   Similar to SSHI but uses a switch to connect the piezo to the storage capacitor.
        *   The `SYNC` controller closes the switch for `ton` (about $\pi\sqrt{LC_p}$).

    *   **Topology 4: FBR with Zener Clamp (Simple).**
        *   FBR failed on $V_{\text{out\_min}}$ for S4 and S2. Just adding a Zener won't help the low-end.

    *   **Refining SSHI for this problem:**
        *   To maximize $V_{\text{out}}$ and minimize startup time, we need to invert the voltage on $C_p$.
        *   Standard Parallel SSHI: $L$ and $S$ are in parallel with the piezo. When $S$ closes, $C_p$ oscillates with $L$ and the voltage flips.
        *   Circuit:
            *   Piezo between `pzp` and `pzn`.
            *   Rectifier: $D_1$ (`pzp` $\to$ `out`), $D_2$ (`pzn` $\to$ `out`)? No, that's not a rectifier.
            *   Standard full bridge: $D_1$ (`pzp`, `out`), $D_2$ (`pzn`, `out`), $D_3$ (`0`, `pzp`), $D_4$ (`0`, `pzn`).
            *   Wait, the prompt says: "full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"]".
            *   SSHI part: $L_1$ between `pzp` and `n1`, $S_1$ between `n1` and `pzn`. `SYNC` controller $G_1$ triggers $S_1$.
            *   This flips the voltage across the piezo terminals.
            *   Add a Zener clamp: $D_z$ (`0`, `out`) model `DZ33`.
            *   Add a storage capacitor: $C_{\text{out}}$ (`out`, `0`).

    *   *Design 1: Parallel SSHI with Full Bridge and Zener.*
        *    Components: 4 diodes (FBR), 1 inductor, 1 switch, 1 SYNC, 1 Zener, 1 capacitor.
        *   Total components: 9.
        *   S1: `pzp` $\to$ `out` (DSCH)
        *   S2: `pzn` $\to$ `out` (DSCH)
        *   S3: `0` $\to$ `pzp` (DSCH)
        *   S4: `0` $\to$ `pzn` (DSCH)
        *   L1: `pzp` $\to$ `n1`
        *   S1: `n1` $\to$ `pzn` (ctrl: G1)
        *   G1: `SYNC`, `edges`: "both", `ton` $\approx \pi\sqrt{LC_p}$
        *   Dz: `0` $\to$ `out` (DZ33)
        *   Cout: `out` $\to$ `0`

    *   *Design 2: SSHI with Half Bridge (if possible).*
        *   If we ground `pzn`, we can use a simpler rectifier. But `pzn` is part of the piezo.
        *   Let's stick to the full bridge for now.

    *   *Design 3: Standard SSHI with a capacitor-based voltage doubler?*
        *   No, the `SYNC` controller is best used for $L$-$C_p$ inversion.

    *   *Checking S3 (Strong Excitation):*
        *   The Zener `DZ33` will clamp `out` to $3.3\text{ V}$, which is $\le 3.6\text{ V}$. OK.

    *   *Checking S4 (Weak Excitation):*
        *   SSHI increases the voltage extracted from the piezo, helping it reach $1.8\text{ V}$ more easily than FBR.

    *   *Checking Ripple:*
        *   $V_{\text{pp}} \le 0.02\text{ V}$. This is very strict. We need a large $C_{\text{out}}$.
        *   $C_{\text{out}}$ max value is $47\text{ \mu F}$. Let's start with something large like $22\text{ \mu F}$ or $47\text{ \mu F}$.

    *   *Checking Startup:*
        *   $t_{\text{up}} \le 0.15\text{ s}$. SSHI generally speeds up charging.

    *   *Checking "Settled":*
        *   $\Delta V \le 0.01\text{ V}$. This requires the energy harvested to balance the load $R_L$ well.

    *   $C_p = 25\text{ nF}$
    *   $L = 10\text{ mH}$ (random start, optimizer will tune)
    *   $t_{\text{on}} = \pi \sqrt{L C_p} = \pi \sqrt{10^{-2} \cdot 25 \cdot 10^{-9}} = \pi \sqrt{2.5 \cdot 10^{-10}} \approx 3.14 \cdot 1.58 \cdot 10^{-5} \approx 49\text{ \mu s}$.
    *   Let's use $t_{\text{on}} = 50\text{ \mu s}$.

    *   Design 1: Full-Bridge + SSHI (Parallel) + Zener.
    *   Design 2: Half-Bridge + SSHI (Parallel) + Zener. (Wait, half-bridge requires a center-tap or a capacitor. Let's try a different approach for Design 2).
    *   Design 2: Full-Bridge + SSHI (Parallel) without Zener, but maybe using a different SYNC configuration (e.g., `edges: pos`) to see if it's more stable? No, "both" is better for SSHI.
    *   Design 3: Let's try a "Series SSHI" like structure. In series SSHI, the inductor is in series with the piezo.
        *   $L_1$ between `pzp` and `n1`.
        *   $S_1$ between `n1` and `out`.
        *   $D_1$ (`n1` to `out`) - no, that's not right.
        *   Actually, the Parallel SSHI is much more common and effective for this.

    *   Let's try a Variation for Design 2: Instead of a Full-Bridge, use a "Half-Bridge" with a large capacitor to create a virtual ground.
        *   $C_{\text{mid}}$ from `pzn` to `0`.
        *   $D_1$ (`pzp` to `out`).
        *   $S_1$, $L_1$ to flip `pzp` and `pzn`.
        *   This might be too simple.

    *   Let's try Design 2 as a "Synchronous Rectifier" where the SYNC closes switches instead of diodes.
        *   $S_1$ (`pzp`, `out`), $S_2$ (`pzn`, `out`), $S_3$ (`0`, `pzp`), $S_4$ (`0`, `pzn`).
        *   But we only have 4 switches and 2 SYNCs. Not enough for a full synchronous rectifier.

    *   Let's stick to:
        1. Parallel SSHI + Full Bridge + Zener (Robust)
        2. Parallel SSHI + Full Bridge (No Zener, but maybe different values) -> Actually, the prompt says "different connectivity". So let's try a different rectifier.
        3. Parallel SSHI + Half Bridge (Piezo `pzn` grounded via a capacitor) + Zener.

    *   Wait, let's refine the "Half-Bridge" (Design 2):
        *   Piezo is between `pzp` and `pzn`.
        *   $C_{\text{split}}$ from `pzn` to `0`.
        *   $D_1$ (`pzp`, `out`).
        *   $D_2$ (`pzn`, `out`)? No.
        *   Let's try a simpler approach:
            Design 1: `FBR + SSHI_L + Zener`
            Design 2: `FBR + SSHI_L` (No Zener, different structure) -> No, just try `Half-Bridge + SSHI_L + Zener`.
            Design 3: `FBR + SSHI_L` but with a different switch placement.

    *   Let's reconsider the Zener. $V_{\text{out\_max}} = 3.6\text{ V}$. S3 has $V_{\text{oc\_amp}} \approx 6.4\text{ V}$ (since $I_p = 100\text{ uA}$). FBR on S3 gave $5.7\text{ V}$. $5.7\text{ V}$ is $> 3.6\text{ V}$. A Zener is mandatory.

    *   Let's refine Design 2 (Half-Bridge):
        *   `pzn` connected to `0` via $C_1$.
        *   $D_1$ (`pzp`, `out`).
        *   $L_1$ (`pzp`, `n1`), $S_1$ (`n1`, `pzn`).
        *   $C_{\text{out}}$ (`out`, `0`).
        *   $D_z$ (`0`, `out`).
        *   This uses the capacitor $C_1$ to maintain a virtual ground at `pzn`.

    *   Design 3: What about a "voltage doubler" with SSHI?
        *   SSHI usually just enhances the voltage of the source. A doubler could push $V_{\text{out}}$ higher, but we already have overvoltage issues in S3.

    *   Let's go with:
        1.  `pzp` $\to$ `out` (D1), `pzn` $\to$ `out` (D2), `0` $\to$ `pzp` (D3), `0` $\to$ `pzn` (D4) [FBR]
            `pzp` $\to$ `n1` (L1), `n1` $\to$ `pzn` (S1, ctrl: G1) [SSHI]
            `out` $\to$ `0` (Cout), `0` $\to$ `out` (Dz) [Filter/Clamp]
        2.  `pzp` $\to$ `out` (D1), `pzn` $\to$ `0` (C1) [Half-Bridge]
            `pzp` $\to$ `n1` (L1), `n1` $\to$ `pzn` (S1, ctrl: G1) [SSHI]
            `out` $\to$ `0` (Cout), `0` $\to$ `out` (Dz) [Filter/Clamp]
        3.  `pzp` $\to$ `out` (D1), `pzn` $\to$ `out` (D2), `0` $\to$ `pzp` (D3), `0` $\to$ `pzn` (D4) [FBR]
            `pzp` $\to$ `n1` (L1), `n1` $\to$ `pzn` (S1, ctrl: G1) [SSHI]
            `out` $\to$ `n2` (L2), `n2` $\to$ `0` (S2, ctrl: G2) [L-C output filter/buck-like? No, that's too complex].
            Let's try another SSHI variant: Two inductors? No.
            Let's try the FBR + SSHI, but replace the FBR with a simpler 2-diode rectifier (Half-wave).
            `pzp` $\to$ `out` (D1), `pzn` $\to$ `0` (D2) [Half-wave]
            `pzp` $\to$ `n1` (L1), `n1` $\to$ `pzn` (S1, ctrl: G1) [SSHI]
            `out` $\to$ `0` (Cout), `0` $\to$ `out` (Dz) [Filter/Clamp]

    *   Wait, the most effective SSHI is often the one that flips the voltage across $C_p$.
        Let's double-check the FBR connection.
        $D_1$: `pzp` $\to$ `out`
        $D_2$: `pzn` $\to$ `out`
        $D_3$: `0` $\to$ `pzp`
        $D_4$: `0` $\to$ `pzn`
        If $V_{\text{pzp}} > V_{\text{out}}$ and $V_{\text{pzn}} < 0$, $D_1$ and $D_4$ conduct.
        If $V_{\text{pzp}} < 0$ and $V_{\text{pzn}} > V_{\text{out}}$, $D_2$ and $D_3$ conduct.
        This is a standard full bridge.

    *   $C_{\text{out}} = 47\text{ \mu F}$ (Maximized to minimize ripple).
    *   $L_1 = 10\text{ mH}$.
    *   $t_{\text{on}} = 50\text{ \mu s}$.
    *   $G_1$: `edges` = "both", `phase` = 0.

    *   The "settled" condition ($\Delta V \le 0.01\text{ V}$) is the hardest. It means the energy extracted must exactly match the energy consumed by $R_L$ (and the SYNC controller).
    *   The "ripple" condition ($V_{\text{pp}} \le 0.02\text{ V}$) is also very strict. A large $C_{\text{out}}$ is essential.

    *   *Design 1: Parallel SSHI + FBR + Zener*
        *   D1: `pzp`, `out` (DSCH)
        *   D2: `pzn`, `out` (DSCH)
        *   D3: `0`, `pzp` (DSCH)
        *   D4: `0`, `pzn` (DSCH)
        *   L1: `pzp`, `n1` (10mH)
        *   S1: `n1`, `pzn` (ctrl: G1)
        *   G1: SYNC (ton=50u, phase=0, edges="both")
        *   Dz: `0`, `out` (DZ33)
        *   Cout: `out`, `0` (47uF)

    *   *Design 2: Parallel SSHI + Half-Bridge (with $C_{\text{split}}$) + Zener*
        *   D1: `pzp`, `out` (DSCH)
        *   Csplit: `pzn`, `0` (47uF)
        *   L1: `pzp`, `n1` (10mH)
        *   S1: `n1`, `pzn` (ctrl: G1)
        *   G1: SYNC (ton=50u, phase=0, edges="both")
        *   Dz: `0`, `out` (DZ33)
        *   Cout: `out`, `0` (47uF)

    *   *Design 3: Parallel SSHI + Half-Wave Rectifier + Zener*
        *   D1: `pzp`, `out` (DSCH)
        *   D2: `0`, `pzn` (DSCH)
        *   L1: `pzp`, `n1` (10mH)
        *   S1: `n1`, `pzn` (ctrl: G1)
        *   G1: SYNC (ton=50u, phase=0, edges="both")
        *   Dz: `0`, `out` (DZ33)
        *   Cout: `out`, `0` (47uF)

    Wait, for Design 2, the capacitor `Csplit` from `pzn` to `0` will charge up to $V_{\text{out}}/2$. This is a common trick to replace two diodes with one.

    Let's double check the components count:
    Design 1: 4D + 1L + 1S + 1SYNC + 1D(Z) + 1C = 9 components. (Limit 16) - OK.

    Wait, one more check on the SYNC controller: "closes its switches for 'ton' seconds ... at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero crossings of the piezo current."
    For SSHI, you want to flip the voltage when the voltage is at its peak (which is when the current is zero). This matches the SYNC controller's behavior.
